title: How Albert Einstein's Brain Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the afterlife of Albert Einstein's brain. Einstein was cremated, but pathologist Thomas Harvey, who performed the autopsy at Princeton Hospital, kept the brain. Harvey photographed and sectioned it, sent pieces to researchers, and became obsessed with it, living reclusively with it for decades. Dr. Marian Diamond's study of glial cells found Einstein had a higher glial-to-neuron ratio, but her methodology was flawed (age, no IQ data, discarded measurements). Dr. Sandra Witelson at McMaster University later reported Einstein's parietal lobe was about 15 percent wider and that his Sylvian fissure was absent or not pronounced, a finding that remains unproven. Molly Edmonds raised the ethical concern that labeling such differences as damage could have limited Einstein's education. Harvey returned the brain to Princeton before dying in 2007. The episode closes with a correction about Jelly Belly booger-flavored beans and promos for the brainSTUFF podcast.

segments.title: Opening banter and Einstein's cremation
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about brain size, then discuss Einstein's wish to be cremated and not worshipped, and that his brain was kept after cremation.

segments.title: Thomas Harvey takes the brain
segments.summary: Pathologist Thomas Harvey, performing Einstein's autopsy at Princeton Hospital, removed and kept the brain instead of cremating it. Chuck recounts a story about seeing a head in a bucket.

segments.title: Harvey's study and sending brain pieces to researchers
segments.summary: Harvey photographed and measured the brain, found it looked average, cut it into pieces, and sent them to researchers worldwide while waiting for results. He became reclusive and kept the brain in unusual places.

segments.title: Marian Diamond's glial cell study and its flaws
segments.summary: Marian Diamond at UC Berkeley, known for rat brain plasticity work, reported Einstein had a higher ratio of glial cells. Hosts point out flaws: Einstein was older than the comparison brains, IQ was not considered, and she discarded measurements that did not fit.

segments.title: Witelson's parietal lobe findings
segments.summary: Sandra Witelson at McMaster University, after a tip from Britt Anderson, reported Einstein's parietal lobe was about 15 percent wider and that his Sylvian fissure was absent or not pronounced. Hosts note this is a benchmark awaiting future verification.

segments.title: Ethics of labeling brain differences
segments.summary: Molly Edmonds raises the concern that calling Einstein's brain differences damage could have discouraged his education. Hosts note his delayed speech and address-writing habit.

segments.title: Harvey's later years and return of the brain
segments.summary: Harvey died in 2007 at age 94 and had returned the brain to Princeton Hospital, where it was left to the resident pathologist. A book, Driving with Mr. Albert, by Michael Paterniti covers Harvey's road trips with the brain.

segments.title: Correction: Jelly Belly booger beans
segments.summary: Hosts correct an earlier claim after listener Misha Bailey pointed out that Jelly Belly does make booger-flavored jelly beans, as part of its Bean Boozled-style special edition.

segments.title: Promo and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts promote the brainSTUFF podcast and its hot dog episode, invite listener email, and close the episode.
